set_title: Polyuria, thirst and a sodium problem
stem: A 26-year-old man with schizophrenia passes large volumes of urine. Serum sodium is 130 mEq/L and urine osmolality is 70 mOsm/kg. After a supervised night without water, urine osmolality is 620 mOsm/kg.
oneliner: 26M + schizophrenia + polyuria + Na 130 + urine osm 70 → 620 after a night without water → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Central DI keeps the urine **dilute when water is withheld**; his reached 620 mOsm/kg
whyNot.C: Nephrogenic DI also keeps the urine **dilute without water**, and gives a high sodium, not 130
whyNot.D: SIADH makes the urine **concentrated at baseline**; his was 70 mOsm/kg
whyNot.E: Osmotic diuresis needs **glucose in the urine**; nothing here suggests it, and urine of 70 is far too dilute

why: Drinking too much lowers the sodium and suppresses ADH, so the urine is dilute. **Once water is withheld, ADH rises and the urine concentrates normally**, which proves both the pituitary and the kidney work.

head: Serum sodium
Urine at baseline
Water deprivation, then desmopressin
Typical setting
rows: **Stays dilute without water, then rises by more than 50% after desmopressin**
**Stays dilute even after desmopressin** (ADH already high)
**Concentrates when water is withheld**; little further rise with desmopressin
**Inappropriately concentrated (above 100 mOsm/kg) with urine sodium above 40 mEq/L**
Small cell lung cancer, CNS disease, drugs; euvolemic
**Glucose in the urine**; osmolality near plasma, not very dilute

idea.rule: Low sodium + dilute urine that concentrates without water = the patient is drinking too much.
also: Long-standing polydipsia washes out the medullary gradient, so the rise can be blunted

set_title: Low blood glucose with sweating or confusion: whose insulin, or no insulin at all
stem: A 27-year-old woman who does not have diabetes has recurrent episodes of sweating and confusion. During an episode, glucose is 32 mg/dL and serum insulin is high. A sulfonylurea screen is negative. C-peptide is low.
oneliner: 27F + no diabetes + recurrent sweating and confusion + glucose 32 mg/dL + high insulin + negative screen + low C-peptide → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Sulfonylureas raise C-peptide and the screen is positive; hers is **low** and the screen is **negative**
whyNot.C: Von Gierke disease has low insulin; hers is **high**
whyNot.D: Insulin excess from treatment needs known diabetes; she **does not have diabetes**
whyNot.E: Insulinoma makes insulin with C-peptide, so C-peptide is high; hers is **low**

why: Injected insulin raises the insulin level, while the pancreas senses the low glucose and shuts off its own secretion, so C-peptide and proinsulin are low. **High insulin with a low C-peptide and a negative screen** in a patient without diabetes means self-injected insulin.

head: Insulin
C-peptide and proinsulin
Sulfonylurea screen
Lactate, liver and setting
rows: Fasting hypoglycemia relieved by glucose; beta-cell tumor of the pancreas
No diabetes; access to insulin, as in a health care worker
**Known diabetes on insulin** with an extra dose, a missed meal or exercise
**Lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hypertriglyceridemia and a large liver** since infancy

idea.rule: High insulin with a low C-peptide means the insulin came from outside.
also: C-peptide is co-secreted with endogenous insulin
Commercial insulin assays may not detect some analogs
Factitious disorder is more common in health care workers

set_title: Low blood glucose with sweating or confusion: whose insulin, or no insulin at all
stem: A 6-year-old girl has recurrent hypoglycemia that resolves with intravenous dextrose. Insulin given by a caregiver and von Gierke disease are both being considered.
oneliner: 6F + recurrent hypoglycemia + resolves with dextrose → Insulin given by a caregiver or von Gierke disease?
ask: Which single finding favours insulin given by a caregiver over von Gierke disease?

options.A: Glucose below 40 mg/dL during an episode
options.D: High serum insulin with a low C-peptide
options.E: Episodes that keep recurring over several months

whyNot.A: Both drop glucose low enough to cause symptoms, so the value does not separate them
whyNot.B: Dextrose corrects the low glucose in **both**
whyNot.C: Adrenergic symptoms follow low glucose from **any** cause

answer: High serum insulin with a low C-peptide
why: Both cause recurrent hypoglycemia that dextrose reverses. In von Gierke disease insulin is appropriately low, whereas injected insulin gives **high insulin with a low C-peptide**; this pattern in a child should prompt a report for factitious disorder imposed on another.

head: Insulin
C-peptide and proinsulin
Sulfonylurea screen
Lactate, liver and setting
rows: Fasting hypoglycemia relieved by glucose; beta-cell tumor of the pancreas
No diabetes; access to insulin, as in a health care worker
**Known diabetes on insulin** with an extra dose, a missed meal or exercise
**Lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hypertriglyceridemia and a large liver** since infancy

idea.rule: Hypoglycemia with high insulin and low C-peptide in a child means someone is injecting insulin.
also: Von Gierke disease adds lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hypertriglyceridemia and a large liver
Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency blocks the last step of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis
The physician must report suspected abuse

set_title: Vomiting, deep breathing or coma with ketones: diabetic ketoacidosis or a look-alike
stem: A 41-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 1 day of vomiting and abdominal pain. He drank heavily for 2 weeks and has eaten almost nothing for 4 days. He has no history of diabetes. Respirations are deep and rapid. Serum glucose is 82 mg/dL, arterial pH is 7.17, serum bicarbonate is 9 mEq/L, and serum beta-hydroxybutyrate is markedly raised.
oneliner: 41M + 2 weeks of heavy drinking, little food for 4 days + vomiting and deep rapid breathing + glucose 82 + pH 7.17 + bicarbonate 9 + high beta-hydroxybutyrate → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Hyperosmolar state needs a glucose above 600 mg/dL and a normal pH; his glucose is **82 mg/dL** and his pH **7.17**
whyNot.B: Diabetic ketoacidosis requires hyperglycemia in a diabetic patient; he has **no diabetes** and a glucose of **82 mg/dL**
whyNot.C: Starvation ketosis is mild, with bicarbonate usually above 18 mEq/L; his bicarbonate is **9** with a pH of **7.17**
whyNot.D: Insulin excess lowers glucose and blocks ketones; he has **no diabetes** and a **bicarbonate of 9** with a raised beta-hydroxybutyrate

why: Heavy drinking with several days of starvation depletes glycogen, and ethanol metabolism raises the NADH to NAD+ ratio, which pushes acetoacetate toward beta-hydroxybutyrate. **Anion gap ketoacidosis with a normal or low glucose after a binge** is alcoholic ketoacidosis; treat with saline, dextrose and thiamine.

head: Glucose
pH and bicarbonate
Ketones
Serum osmolality
Typical patient and trigger
rows: Type 1 diabetes with missed insulin or an infection
pH above 7.30 and bicarbonate above 18 mEq/L
Older adult with type 2 diabetes, infection and poor fluid intake
Anion gap acidosis, often mixed with a vomiting alkalosis
Large beta-hydroxybutyrate; nitroprusside test may read weak
**Heavy drinking, then vomiting and days without food**
**Mild: bicarbonate usually above 18 mEq/L, pH near normal**
Insulin or sulfonylurea excess, with sweating and tremor

idea.rule: Ketoacidosis with a normal glucose after a binge = alcoholic ketoacidosis; with a very high glucose = DKA.
also: Vomiting adds a metabolic alkalosis, so the pH can be higher than the gap suggests
Dextrose stimulates insulin and clears the ketones
Give thiamine before or with glucose

set_title: Periods stopped, with or without milky discharge: pituitary, drug, thyroid, energy deficit or ovary
stem: A 29-year-old woman has had amenorrhea for 4 months and a milky discharge from both breasts; a pregnancy test is negative. She started risperidone 3 months ago. Her serum prolactin is 62 ng/mL and her TSH is normal.
oneliner: 29F + amenorrhea for 4 months + bilateral milky discharge + negative pregnancy test + risperidone started 3 months ago + prolactin 62 ng/mL + normal TSH → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: It follows postpartum hemorrhage and gives a **low prolactin** with failure to lactate; she has **galactorrhea** and a **high prolactin**
whyNot.C: A raised TRH can lift prolactin, but her **TSH is normal**
whyNot.D: It does not raise prolactin or cause **galactorrhea**; hers is **62 ng/mL** with a milky discharge
whyNot.E: An adenoma gives the same picture, but a **dopamine antagonist started 3 months ago** already explains the prolactin

why: Risperidone blocks D2 receptors on lactotrophs and removes the dopamine brake on prolactin. A **new dopamine antagonist** (risperidone, metoclopramide) explains the high prolactin, galactorrhea and amenorrhea, and stopping or switching the drug reverses it.

head: Prolactin
FSH and LH
TSH
Clincher
rows: No drug or thyroid cause; MRI shows a pituitary adenoma; treat with a dopamine agonist
**Dopamine antagonist** (risperidone, metoclopramide); prolactin falls when the drug stops
Raised TRH also stimulates lactotrophs; levothyroxine corrects the prolactin
Low weight and heavy training; low estradiol, low bone density, stress fractures
Postpartum hemorrhage with failure to lactate; low ACTH and cortisol cause orthostasis
Hot flashes and vaginal dryness; the ovary no longer makes estrogen or inhibin

idea.rule: High prolactin: no drug and normal TSH = tumor; dopamine antagonist = drug; high TSH = thyroid.
also: Metoclopramide also blocks D2 and raises prolactin
Aripiprazole, a partial agonist, is the antipsychotic least likely to do this
Check for pregnancy and TSH before blaming the drug
